A 1964 study of 48 large American cities revealed that on the average, industrial land use accounted for 8.6% of total land area whereas commercial land use accounted for 3.7% of total land area. 16/ Another study indicates that vacant land in central cities is fast disappearing. 17/ When cities cannot aprawl, urban growth can be sustained only by an increase in density, or by consumption of more space at peripheral areas.
The recognition of existence and importance of economic interactions/\ninterrelations among base cities, adjacent communities, and peripheral developments is evidenced by the establishment of substate/regional agencies or councils
which have proliferated partly in response to Federal actions. Twenty-four major
Federal grant programs (in 1973) provide assistance specifically for planning. Ten
of the programs supported or required planning on a multi-jutisdictional basis to
qualify for grants. By the end of 1973, there were over 600 Councils of Government
(COG's). Forty-four states had delineated substate districting systems, with a total
of 488 districts. Approximately $350 million was available in FY 1973 in Federal
grants--$100 million for comprehensive planning and management and $250 million
for functional planning. A large share of these funds were utilized by substate
districts. 18/ The districts are often called planning regions or planning districts.
The COG's and planning regions as well as municipal/county planning units perform planning in regard to overall land use and relation of living/work places, industrial growth and location, transportation systems, drainage/flood control, air/water pollution, nature/parks/open spaces, new town locations/sizes, racial issues, destratification, population distribution, and other issues. 19/ Most of the land-use maps used in the preparation of Table 6 in this report were prepared by municipal/regional planning groups while conducting projects partly financed by the Department of Housing and Urban Development.
